p.bold: Truly Functional Solutions to the Longest Uptrend Problem

body.p: ALEXANDER DINGES , RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau, Germany RALF HINZE , RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau, Germany

Solutions to the longest increasing subsequence problem are typically implemented imperatively, relying on arrays for constant-time lookups and updates. Replacing these arrays with functional sequences allows a purely functional solution with the same asymptotic running time, but with significantly worse practical performance. In this pearl, we present a purely functional approach that is not only asymptotically optimal, but also efficient in practice. The core idea is to exploit the interplay between search, lookup, and update operations through Huet’s zipper. In addition, we improve the adaptive behaviour of imperative solutions commonly found in the literature.

CCS Concepts: • Theory of computation → Data structures design and analysis ; • Software and its
engineering → Functional languages .
Additional Key Words and Phrases: Longest Increasing Subsequence, Zipper, Haskell

ACM Reference Format: Alexander Dinges and Ralf Hinze. 2025. Truly Functional Solutions to the Longest Uptrend Problem (Functional Pearl). Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 9, ICFP, Article 251 (August 2025), 16 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3747520

sec.title: 1 Introduction
sec.p: I can resist anything except temptation. Oscar Wilde, Lady Windermere’s Fan

“Shall I be pure or impure?” Many temptations lure the functional programmer: input/output, exceptions, references, and, in particular, arrays with constant-time update. And the sirens whisper: “Haskell is the world’s finest imperative programming language.” We openly admit that we too have succumbed to temptation: on more than one occasion, the efficiency promises of updatable arrays have been too compelling. Here is a recent example. We derived an algorithm for solving the “longest increasing subsequence” problem. Briefly, given a sequence of elements, the problem is to find a longest subsequence that is strictly increasing. A subsequence is given by a selection of the original data, such that the relative order of the data items is preserved. The derived algorithm can justifiably be called imperative, and indeed we used the ST -monad for the Haskell implementation. For reference, Figure 1 summarizes the most important facts, using pseudo-code rather than monadic code to emphasize its imperative nature. Indeed, open a classic textbook on program derivation [ 2 , 5 ] and you will find similar solutions. The central operation is an in-place array update:

The candidates are not only arranged in decreasing order of length, but also in increasing order of improvement — the shorter, the better: 𝑖 ≤ 𝑗 = ⇒ 𝑠 [ 𝑖 ] ≼ 𝑠 [ 𝑗 ]. The program maintains this invariant. An example run of the algorithm is shown in Figure 2 .
Fig. 1. An 𝑛 · log 𝑚 algorithm for solving the “longest increasing subsequence” problem.

The details are not important. Suffice it to say that a binary search determines an index, which is then used to read one array element and to update a second. To functionalize the code, we can replace the ephemeral, imperative array with a persistent, functional array, but you might argue that this representation change does not remove the imperative nature.
let i = binary-search · · · in update s ( i −1) ( a : s ! i )

If each operation — search, look-up, and update — runs in logarithmic time, then the asymptotic running time is no worse than that of the imperative fragment. However, the constant factors are worse, as look-up and update do not run in constant-time; and, indeed, benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of the imperative program. We gave up ... but the problem gnawed at us. After a while, we realized that we had been guilty of imperative thinking. The three operations — search, look-up, and update — are closely intertwined, but they communicate rather indirectly via numerical positions, via indices. Surely there is a better way of arranging their interplay. This pearl tells the story of a truly functional solution to the “longest increasing subsequence” problem (“longest uptrend” for short). The motto is “ Down with indices! ” Section 2 introduces the basic idea using the data-structural manifestation of binary search: binary trees. Section 3 addresses the inefficiency of binary trees by introducing a balancing scheme. Finally, Section 4 improves the interface and the implementation. This paper is aimed at readers with a basic understanding of functional programming; no specialized knowledge of algorithm design is presumed.

Given the input sequence [0 , 7 , 4 , 6 , 1 , 5 , 3 , 4 , 1] of length 9, the algorithm returns [0 , 1 , 3 , 4] as its longest increasing subsequence. It starts with an array s of length 10, setting 𝑠 [9] = []. The input sequence is processed in reverse order, updating the array s as follows:

The active part of the array is highlighted in orange. In each step, either a longer uptrend is added at the front or an existing candidate is replaced by an improved one. Only in the latter case, a binary search is performed. Observe that the candidates in each row (and each column) are arranged in increasing order of improvement.
Fig. 2. An example run of Longest-Increasing-Subsequence.

2.4
Longest Uptrend As explained in Figure 1 , the algorithm for solving the “longest uptrend” problem maintains a sequence of candidate solutions arranged in decreasing order of length. Each candidate is the best uptrend (with respect to the improvement relation ≼) among all uptrends of the same length. When every input element has been processed, the leftmost candidate is therefore the longest uptrend (the definition of leftmost is standard and omitted).
best-longest-uptrend :: ( Ord a ) ⇒[ a ] →[ a ] best-longest-uptrend = leftmost · foldr insert ( single [ ])

The best and only uptrend of length 0 is the empty list [ ]. The step function insert first determines a tipping point with respect to the extensibility relation: two adjacent uptrends, say w and v , such that ¬ a − < w and a − < v . Depending on the location of the tipping point, insert then takes one of two actions.

sec.title: 3 Balanced Binary Tree
sec.p: The implementation in Section 2.4 serves mainly as a proof of concept. It has a quadratic worst-case running time Θ( 𝑛 2), because the binary tree always degenerates to a list-like structure, see Figure 3 . However, a fix is easy to find: we impose a balancing scheme. There are a few dozen options to choose from. Since our trees only grow, never shrink, we pick the simplest, and therefore most attractive scheme: Okasaki’s red-black trees ( 1999 ). If you need a refresher, Figure 4 summarizes the key facts about red-black trees.
Continuing the example from Figure 2 , best-longest-uptrend applied to the input [0 , 7 , 4 , 6 , 1 , 5 , 3 , 4 , 1] produces the following sequence of trees (from left to right):
Each tree corresponds to a row in Figure 2 . Sadly, since the trees are always extended on the left, they degenerate to a list-like structure. Thus, binary-search is, in fact, a linear search.

The helper function balance takes a location and maintains the invariant that the focus is coloured red. It walks up the left spine, distinguishing three cases:

Red-black trees are a cunning representation of 2-3-4 trees, where ternary and quaternary nodes are represented by small binary trees consisting of a black root and one or two red children. The relation to 2-3-4 trees motivates the red-condition : a red node can only appear as a child of a black node. 2-3-4 trees are perfectly balanced, motivating the black-condition : on any path from the root to a leaf, the number of black nodes is the same — the number is called the black-height . The two conditions ensure that each path from the root to a leaf has logarithmic length in the total number of nodes.

Insertion works in the same way as with binary trees, except that a leaf is replaced by a red node, possibly violating the red-condition, but not the black-condition. The violation is fixed by local transformations along the search path, as illustrated above. Each rewrite possibly causes a violation further up the tree. If a red node percolates to the top, it is turned into a black node, increasing the black-height by one.
Fig. 4. Red-black trees: a brief summary.

If the parent is black, no (further) re-balancing is necessary. If the parent is red, the red-condition is violated: the red-red-black path is transformed into a red node with two black children, see Figure 4 ; and the re-balancing continues. If there is no parent node, the red node has percolated to the top, where it is re-coloured to be black.

4
Finish: Finger Tree The implementation can be improved in two ways, addressing two orthogonal issues. The first improvement is of algorithmic nature and addresses an efficiency problem. The imperative solution runs in linear time, if the input is sorted or nearly sorted, as the case where the table grows is treated separately (lines 5-7 in Figure 1 ). To achieve the same adaptive behaviour, we need to be able to extend a sequence in amortized constant time and to access the head in constant time. The second improvement concerns a software-engineering issue: the lack of a proper interface. Both the data structures, red-black trees and zippers, and the central algorithm, binary search, are tailored to the application and are of little general use. (The search returns a pointer to a node, revealing implementation details. A malicious adversary could tinker with the internals. Ouch.) We address both problems in turn.

4.1
Left-Spine View Let us start with a crucial observation. Our application is rather special in that new elements are only added at the front. This usage pattern has an interesting consequence: the size of a red-black
tree completely determines its shape [ 6 ]. To see why this is the case, let us consider a few small examples. The diagrams below show the shapes for sizes up to 8. For perspicuity, the insertion path, the so-called left spine , is drawn horizontally (ignore the numbers for the moment).

We observe that red nodes are rather rare; they only appear on the left spine. This is not a coincidence. New nodes, which are coloured red, are placed on the left spine. If the red-condition is violated, the first rewrite rule of Figure 4 fires. The rule is repeated below, but with a twist: in accordance with the examples, the left spine is drawn horizontally.

The rule maintains the invariant that red nodes only appear on the spine. Consequently, the trees hanging from the spine are all black. This has two immediate consequences. First, only the first rule ever fires, see Figure 4 . Second, the black-condition entails that the trees below the spine are perfectly balanced. Thus, the left spine is a sequence of topped perfect trees, so-called pennants . The black-condition also implies that a pennant of height h appears either once or twice. Since the size of a pennant of height h is 2 ℎ , the shape of a tree of size n is uniquely determined by the binary representation of n :

The digit 1 corresponds to a single black pennant, the digit 2 to a red pennant followed by a black pennant, see the examples above. (Note that the digit 0 is not needed in this context.) The weight of the digit equals the size of the pennant(s). Taking the analogy further, the rewrite rule ( 1 ) can be seen as implementing a carry, mapping 1 · 2 𝑖 + 2 · 2 𝑖 to 3 · 2 𝑖 = 1 · 2 𝑖 + 1 · 21+ 𝑖 . The analysis suggests a representation change, switching from the standard representation of red-black trees to the left-spine view .

4.3
Exponential Search Searching a finger tree proceeds in two steps: first, we determine the full binary tree, in which the tipping point is located; then we search this tree. Just as binary trees are the manifestation of binary search , (one-sided) finger trees are the incarnation of exponential search . (If you are curious, you may want to peek ahead at Figure 5 for an illustration of the correspondence.) Thanks to the typed zipper, we can have the search return the position of elements , rather than nodes. A location of an element within a finger tree has type ( a ⇒ Spine a , a ). Loosely speaking, the first component allows us to write a new value to the location, while the second component allows us to read the old value. If we drop one of the components, we obtain read-only or write- only locations. Tailored to our application, exponential search returns the optional left location write-only and the optional right location read-only.

The worker function assumes that the previous element on the spine violates the predicate. It walks along the spine until it finds an element that satisfies it, or until it reaches the end. In both cases, a binary search is subsequently performed using find , introduced further below. Note that the argument of explore is a location on the spine, which enables us to move in both directions. The function rewind makes good use of this feature.

This compares favourably to binary search, which is logarithmic in the size of the entire sequence. In addition, the algorithm shows a nice adaptive behaviour: it finishes in linear time if the sequence is sorted or nearly sorted, for example, for inputs [1 , 2 , . . . , n ] and [2 , 1 , 4 , 3 , 6 , 5 , . . . , n , n −1]. In these cases, exponential search shows its strength — recall that it runs in Θ(log 𝑖 ), where 𝑖 is the position of the tipping point. This also speeds up the invocation of apply , as the zipping function simply walks back along the search path. Moreover, cons runs in amortized constant time. It is also worth noting that the algorithm outperforms the imperative implementation for many inputs. For example, the imperative solution requires Θ( 𝑛 · log 𝑛 ) time for the second example above, as a binary search is performed at every second step. Its logic is, in some sense, too simplistic:

it only works efficiently when new uptrends are added frequently, that is, when the then branch is entered frequently, see Figure 1 . Enough asymptotics, let the numbers speak for themselves: Appendix A shows the results of some micro-benchmarks. Overall, the benchmarks support the results of the asymptotic analysis. Quite pleasingly, the purely functional solutions are on a par with the imperative implementation; in some cases they even outperform the latter thanks to the improved adaptive behaviour. Hurrah!

sec.title: 5 Conclusion
sec.p: All in all, this was an enjoyable exercise in algorithm, data structure, and interface design. Our first attempts at purely functional solutions to the “longest uptrend” problem focused on implementing searchable , indexable sequence types, supporting the following interface.

Sequ :: Type → Type
nil :: Sequ a
cons :: a → Sequ a → Sequ a (!):: Sequ a → Int → a
update :: Sequ a → Int → a → Sequ a
search :: ( a → Bool ) → Sequ a → Int

We tried out several data structures, but the efforts did not pay off. Simply replacing ephemeral arrays with these persistent sequence types worsened the running time by an order of magnitude. Abstracting slightly from the details of our application (renaming Spine to Sequ and a ⇒ Spine a to Pos a ), our finger trees can be used to implement a radically different interface.

Sequ :: Type → Type
nil :: Sequ a
cons :: a → Sequ a → Sequ a
search :: ( a → Bool ) → Sequ a →( Maybe ( Pos a , a ) , Maybe ( Pos a , a )) Pos :: Type → Type
apply :: Pos a → a → Sequ a

The revised interface is much more restrictive, but at the same time also much safer. The indices, the numerical positions, have disappeared from the scene — no “index out of range” errors anymore. Indices are replaced by paths. The function search returns two positions; each of these positions can be “applied” to a value to update the original sequence, replacing the general update mechanism based on numerical positions. This interface works beautifully for the “longest uptrend” problem. Whether it has other uses remains to be seen. We have also gained some algorithmic insights. An important part of the lazy functional DNA is the idea of turning control structures into data structures: binary trees are the manifestation of binary search. Maybe this is old news to you, but it was new to us that finger trees are the incarnation of exponential search. In conclusion, it is pleasing to see that we can keep up with or even surpass the imperative program. But, what was the crucial step in achieving this goal? We say the introduction of Huet’s zipper! This enabled us to organize the interplay of search, look-up, and update much more neatly. So, three cheers to Gérard!

To evaluate the performance of our zipper-based implementations, we benchmark them against a few alternatives. In total, we compare six different implementations.

• ST-Arrays: The imperative solution, see Figure 1 , transliterated into Haskell’s imperative sublanguage, using the ST -monad and ST -arrays. This implementation serves as the baseline for comparison.
• ST-Arrays-Exponential-Search: An adaptation of the imperative solution, that uses expo-nential search instead of binary search to determine the tipping point.

• Random-Access-Lists: A functional variant of the imperative solution, using persistent sequences based on node-oriented random-access lists. Look-up, update, and search are supported in logarithmic time, so the implementation is asymptotically optimal.

• ADwH: An implementation taken from the textbook Algorithm Design with Haskell [ 1 ], which is developed in a series of exercises (11.6–11.8). The solution is based on AVL-trees. Interestingly, it also avoids indices: In the update step, the AVL-tree is split at the tipping point and then merged with the new element replacing the old.

• Zipper-Red-black-Trees: See Section 3 . • Zipper-Finger-Trees: See Section 4 . We test the implementations on five different types of inputs to highlight the strengths and weaknesses of the approaches:

• [1 . . n ]: The adaptive implementations achieve linear running time for sorted inputs. • interleave [2 . . n + 1] [1 . . n ]: The methods that use exponential search finish in linear time, whereas the imperative solution requires linear-logarithmic time.

The results are presented in Figure 6 , where running times (in seconds) are plotted against the lengths of the input lists (scaled by 5 , 000 , 000). The code, which is publicly available [ 4 ], was compiled using GHC 9.10.1 with the -O2 optimization flag turned on. The benchmarks were executed on an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X CPU. The data shows that the zipper-based implementations perform on par with the imperative programs. When adaptivity is advantageous, finger trees outperform the imperative approach. In the case of random inputs, finger trees perform worse than red-black trees due to the additional overhead of the exponential search. Note that node-oriented random-access lists are structurally similar to the finger trees presented in this paper, which is why Random-Access-Lists, Zipper-Finger-Trees, and ST-Arrays-Exponential-Search exhibit the same performance characteristics.
